title: New UK Prime Minister Says He'll Focus on Making Life Cheaper
summary:
Have you ever noticed how expensive things like food and energy can be? The new prime minister of the United Kingdom, Andy Burnham, says he wants to help. At his very first meeting with his top team of ministers, called a cabinet, he told them he wants to be a "cost of living government." That means he wants to make it easier for people to afford everyday things.

Burnham got a round of applause when he walked into the room. He said he wants people to feel "that help is coming" on costs. But there's a catch: to pay for his plans, he wants to stop a project started by the last prime minister, Keir Starmer. That project was a digital ID scheme—a way for people to prove who they are online. Burnham says the money saved can be used for other things.

Not everyone agrees. Darren Jones, who lost his job in the government, said the digital ID plan didn't have its own money anyway, so Burnham needs to find real cash. The opposition Conservative Party also criticized him, saying he's being careless with the country's money.

Burnham's spokesman said the money will come from savings found by different government departments. The new prime minister also made some surprising choices for his team. He picked John Healey to be chancellor—the person in charge of money—even though Healey had quit his old job over a disagreement. Healey promised to be careful with taxes and spending.

Burnham's first big announcement was £340 million (that's about $430 million) over five years to help homeless people. He said ministers need to be ready to move money around to pay for new ideas. The next few days will show what other changes are coming.
why_it_matters: Government decisions about money are like a giant version of your family's budget—small changes can mean help for many people who struggle to afford basic needs.

background_read: The United Kingdom has a prime minister who leads the government with a team of top ministers called the cabinet.
The country has two major parties: the Labour Party and the Conservative Party, who often argue about spending and taxes.

The previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, from the Labour Party, had a plan to create a digital ID system for citizens. Now, the new prime minister, Andy Burnham (also from Labour), wants to cancel that plan and use the money for other priorities like helping the homeless.
Article_Structure: WHO: Andy Burnham, the new prime minister of the United Kingdom
WHAT: He declared a 'cost of living government,' scrapped a digital ID project, and pledged £340 million for homeless support
WHERE: At a cabinet meeting in the UK government
WHY: To lower everyday living costs and redirect money from cancelled projects to urgent social programs

perspectives.description: They welcome any help that makes food and electricity more affordable, seeing the new prime minister's promise as a sign of relief.
They argue that canceling the scheme wastes the work already done and might make it harder for people to prove who they are online in the future.
They question whether the savings from the cancelled project are real or if the government is just moving numbers around without fixing the root problems.
